grupos.reason: The comment describes a concrete failure where late cancellation requests are rejected by SendGrid and reminder emails are delivered for cancelled bookings.
The comment describes a concrete stale-state bug in which successful cache deletion leaves the UI showing an obsolete timestamp and delete action, misleading users about whether cached data exists.
The comment identifies a concrete user-facing localization error in which hard-coded US date ordering can mislead users in other locales about when the cache was last updated.
The comment identifies a concrete false statement in the migration warning that misleads operators about whether existing data makes the migration unsafe.
The comment describes a concrete incorrect availability result: an event extending beyond a host's override is accepted, allowing booking during unavailable time.
The comment describes a concrete incorrect availability result: slots can include a fixed host on a weekday excluded by that host's schedule.

The comment describes a concrete timezone rollover input that reverses the interval and removes valid availability, producing incorrect scheduling results rather than an optional stylistic improvement.
The comment identifies a concrete incorrect availability result: using the slot start for the end boundary allows bookings that extend beyond working hours.
The comment describes a concrete incorrect availability result: reference equality prevents rejecting a zero-length override and can allow a slot on a closed day.
The comment describes a concrete data accuracy bug in which a single signup attempt increments match_count twice, rather than an optional style or refactoring improvement.

The comment identifies a concrete CSRF vulnerability in which an attacker can change a logged-in user's notification preferences through a GET request, rather than an optional style or best-practice improvement.
The comment identifies a concrete misleading confirmation that promises all topic notifications have stopped even though regular notification level still permits mention and reply notifications.
The comment identifies a concrete input with an uppercase hostname that produces an incorrect website display by omitting the path, rather than an optional style improvement.
The comment identifies concrete hosts that the comparison incorrectly treats as related, producing a path-inclusive website label instead of the expected host-only result.
The comment identifies a concrete security disclosure: anonymous responses expose a hidden website's hostname and potentially path through website_name despite the website visibility restriction.
The comment describes a concrete user-facing accessibility regression: dark-theme badge text has insufficient contrast against its background, making notification counts difficult to read.
The comment requests preserving a visual color preference and describes only a paler author link, not a concrete functional failure or loss of readability.
The comment requests a cosmetic color adjustment for consistency with desktop and the previous theme, without describing a functional failure or misleading statement.
The comment requests visual prominence and mobile/desktop styling consistency without describing unreadable text or any concrete functional failure.
The comment describes a concrete wrong-result bug: double interpolation expands variable tokens inside literal variable values, changing the executed query from the non-splitting path.
The comment identifies a concrete functional failure: SQL expressions are always rejected even when their feature flag is enabled.
The comment identifies a concrete performance cost: sequential checks of distinct denied resources each trigger a full permission query and cache rewrite despite a current action-wide cache.
The comment describes a concrete incorrect-result bug in which specific group permission grants are omitted from user counts and database filtering, rather than an optional improvement.
The comment describes a concrete incorrect-result bug where legacy resource-name filtering excludes authorized group members from V2 user searches.
The comment identifies a concrete false statement in the guard's documentation that misleads readers about which distinct permission authorizes managing members.
The comment identifies a concrete false statement in the return documentation, which promises a Stream even though the method returns a Set and thus misleads readers about its contract.
The comment identifies a concrete caller breakage: EC JWK parsing invokes two methods that throw UnsupportedOperationException, preventing ECDSA verification in the standalone client.
The comment identifies a concrete security failure: tied provider priorities can silently select a non-FIPS provider in a deployment expecting FIPS instead of rejecting the mixed classpath.

The comment requests stronger test coverage against hypothetical mutually compensating conversion bugs without identifying an actual incorrect conversion or user-visible failure in the submitted code.
The comment requests removing redundant discarded work as a micro-optimization, without describing any concrete failure or meaningful user-facing performance cost if it remains.

The comment identifies a concrete incorrect conversion in which an oversized INTEGER such as 2^256 + 1 is truncated to 1, changing the supplied signature rather than merely suggesting defensive validation.
The comment identifies concrete quadratic copying and allocation costs on explicitly supported large batches, rather than a speculative concern or a micro-optimization with no real cost.
The comment identifies a concrete tenfold increase in database and filesystem workload across all cleanup jobs, rather than a stylistic preference or speculative micro-optimization.
The comment identifies a concrete false statement about SQLite’s parameter limit that misleads readers, rather than merely requesting an optional documentation improvement.
The comment requests stronger regression-test coverage and describes a hypothetical reversion escaping detection, not a concrete failure in the code being merged.
The comment requests additional test coverage for an exit-status contract and describes only a hypothetical regression, not a concrete failure in the current code.
The comment describes a concrete security failure in which regeneration leaves old local recovery codes valid for authentication, rather than an optional style or defensive improvement.
The comment describes a concrete functional failure: the reconstructed credential loses its ID, preventing CredentialDeleteHelper from resolving it for account deletion.
The comment identifies a concrete security concern—secret-dependent timing in recovery-code authentication comparisons—rather than an optional style or best-practice improvement.
The comment identifies a concrete request path where dereferencing a None member raises AttributeError and breaks audit-log requests even without optimized pagination.
The comment describes a concrete incorrect result: Top N groups are selected by raw counts rather than weighted counts, omitting groups that should rank higher in the upsampled results.
The comment describes a concrete caller-breaking failure where transformAliasToInputFormat=1 changes the result mapping so the serializer cannot retrieve the weighted count for the original axis.

The comment identifies a concrete false claim in the docstring: it promises valid sample rates while the implementation accepts negative, greater-than-one, and non-finite values, misleading test authors.
The comment describes a concrete correctness failure in offset committing for skipped Kafka offsets and a contradiction with the added tests, rather than an optional style or coverage improvement.
The comment identifies a concrete false-positive test that misses failed-message commits, allowing an unsafe offset advance and potential message loss rather than merely requesting extra coverage.
The comment identifies a concrete shutdown failure in which setting the worker shutdown flag abandons queued messages, while the test falsely appears to verify graceful shutdown.
The comment requests stronger ordering test coverage without identifying a concrete failure in the strategy itself, so ignoring it does not change runtime behavior.
The comment requests stronger concurrency test coverage without identifying a concrete failure in the implementation, so ignoring it does not itself break behavior.

The comment identifies a concrete contract regression: callers configuring a smaller max_segment_spans can now receive segments exceeding that limit because enforcement was replaced by a hard-coded 1000-span cap.
The comment describes a concrete data-loss failure in which merging and unlinking identical keys deletes the buffered segment, rather than an optional improvement.
